lesson.title: From Bunker Hill to Yorktown: The War's Turning Points
lesson.summary: The Revolutionary War stretched across eight years and thirteen colonies, and a handful of pivotal battles, from Bunker Hill to Saratoga to Yorktown, determined its ultimate outcome.
lesson.body:
The fighting that began at Lexington and Concord in April 1775 quickly grew into a full scale war, and the Second Continental Congress's new Continental Army faced its first major test just two months later. On June 17, 1775, colonial forces occupied high ground overlooking Boston, and although the resulting fight is remembered as the Battle of Bunker Hill, most of the combat actually took place on the adjacent Breed's Hill. British troops eventually took the position after three costly assaults, but only after suffering severe casualties, proving that colonial militia could inflict real damage on professional soldiers even in defeat.

After British forces evacuated Boston in early 1776, the war shifted toward New York and New Jersey, where Washington's army suffered a string of defeats and retreats. Morale reached a low point by December 1776, when Washington famously led his troops across the icy Delaware River to launch a surprise attack on Trenton, New Jersey, on December 26, capturing a garrison of Hessian soldiers and reviving flagging American spirits at a moment when many enlistments were about to expire. A follow up victory at Princeton in early January 1777 reinforced the sense that the Continental Army could still fight effectively against professional European troops.

The war's clearest turning point came at Saratoga, New York, in the fall of 1777, where American forces surrounded and forced the surrender of a British army under General John Burgoyne in October. Saratoga convinced France that the Americans had a real chance of winning, and it led directly to a formal alliance between France and the United States in early 1778, bringing French money, soldiers, and, crucially, a navy into the war on the American side.

The war's focus later shifted to the southern colonies, where British forces captured Charleston and Camden but suffered a serious setback at the Battle of Cowpens in South Carolina in January 1781, and were further worn down at Guilford Courthouse in North Carolina that March, a costly victory that left British forces too weakened to hold the region. These southern campaigns pushed British General Charles Cornwallis northward into Virginia in search of a stronger position.

The war's decisive final battle came at Yorktown, Virginia, in the fall of 1781. Washington's Continental Army, joined by French troops under the Comte de Rochambeau, marched south and trapped Cornwallis's army against the coast, while a French fleet under the Comte de Grasse blocked British ships from rescuing him by sea. After a siege of several weeks, Cornwallis surrendered on October 19, 1781. Although the war did not formally end until the Treaty of Paris in 1783, Yorktown effectively convinced Britain that the war could not be won, closing the military chapter of the Revolution that had opened at Lexington and Concord more than six years earlier.
